meta.title: Chinese politics knowledge network, c. 1986-2026
meta.description: Key works and debates on Chinese politics: elite and cadre politics, central-local relations and the policy process, responsiveness, information control, contention and repression, legitimacy and nationalism, political economy, corruption and law, civil society, environment, historical legacies, the periphery and China in the world. Seeds come from this repo's papers.json; works shared with the other maps are imported from them; others are top-cited 2006-2026 articles selected via Crossref (including six China-studies journals) plus anchoring books. Direction: source (later or dependent work) -> target (earlier or anchoring work).

edge_types.builds_on: source extends or relies on target's argument or evidence
edge_types.challenges: source contests target's claim, mechanism or evidence
edge_types.qualifies: source adds a scope condition or moderating factor to target
edge_types.extends_to_new_case: source applies target's logic to a new population, period or domain
edge_types.synthesizes: source integrates target with other work
edge_types.mechanism_tested_by: source tests a mechanism implied by target

meta.verification: Repo works come from the user's Zotero library. Works shared with the other four maps keep their earlier verification. Crossref-selected works take title, authors, year, venue and DOI from Crossref records. All new anchors were found in Crossref, books mostly via published reviews or chapter records. One-line claims for non-repo works are my summaries.

edges.why: Both show how Leninist institutions structure behavior, Walder in the factory and Lieberthal and Oksenberg in bureaucratic policymaking.
Local state corporatism as a product of fiscal decentralization.
Rural industrialization driven by local officials.
Experimentation under hierarchy, not just bargaining.
Decentralization coexists with central cadre control.
Disaggregates the party-state to show central and local agencies pursued different aims around WTO entry, in the fragmented authoritarianism tradition.
Local state corporatism, not only household reform, drove rural growth.
Career incentives in the Great Leap Forward.
Patronage over performance for provincial leaders.
Uses an experiment to probe the limits of the consultative responsiveness described in his book.
Repression of organized participation under Xi.
Lineages enable collective action for public goods.
Business lobbying in the policy process.
Censorship targets collective action, not criticism.
Porous censorship through friction and flooding.
Censorship targets collective action within networked authoritarianism.
Government-paid posts distract rather than argue.
Censorship varies by issue and time.
Collective-action censorship during a nationalist crisis.
From bargaining by riot to party-led bargaining.
Trust in the center among petitioners.
Environmental protest and the policy process.
Theorizes how threat perceptions shape coercive institutions, a framework for the security state Wang and Minzner document.
Preventive repression and surveillance in Xinjiang.
From graduated control to consultative authoritarianism.
Mutual endangerment of party and capital.
Sino-capitalism as an alternative economic model.
Real popular support for the regime.
Survival strategies of a sophisticated autocracy.
Historical memory education shapes Chinese nationalism.
Explains Beijing's use of force through its reading of power trends, adding to debates on whether China is a status quo power.
Private rural entrepreneurs, not local states, drove growth.
Entrepreneurs as allies of the state.
Party-state capitalism at home and state-owned firms abroad.
Party-state capitalism and precarious business-state ties.
Corruption followed growth and was contained.
Anticorruption campaigns and growth amid corruption.
Civil society growth after the 2008 earthquake.
The weakness of the imperial state.
Brings the study of popular contention to semi-democratic Hong Kong, where activism spreads through street politics rather than rightful claims.
Territorial disputes and the use of force.
China in a world of orders.
Domestic sources of China's order engagement.
Domestic politics behind China's strategy toward the order.
China defends autocracy without systematically promoting it.
Both link trade with China to political alignment; Fuchs and Klann show exports fall after leaders meet the Dalai Lama.
State control of commercial actors in economic statecraft.
Shows the AIIB works as an outside option that pushes the World Bank to loosen its lending terms, building on the idea of Chinese finance as a no-strings alternative.
Finds China secures energy mostly through markets rather than state-directed mercantilism, limiting how far commercial actors serve state strategy.
Argues China's industrial policy and IP strategy still erode US structural power even where military-technological imitation has limits.
Land as the base of local state power.
Hollow rural state after tax reform.
Shows hukou reforms left core barriers to migrants in place, a people-side counterpart to Hsing's land-driven account of urbanization.
Pushes fragmented-authoritarian bargaining down to township cadres, who execute hard, promotion-linked targets and shelve unrewarded mandates.
Smith's hollow rural state rests on O'Brien and Li's finding that cadre evaluation drives selective implementation of central policy.
Expands the article's account of the post-1991 Patriotic Education Campaign into a full theory of historical memory and humiliation in Chinese politics.
Shows that very high trust in Beijing reported in surveys like Shi's softens once hierarchical trust is measured carefully across five national surveys.
Locates reform dynamism in entrepreneurs' informal coping institutions that officials tolerate, shifting weight from local-state corporatism to bottom-up adaptation.
The book generalizes the adaptive-informal-institutions argument to explain why China's capitalists do not demand democracy.
Finds party control over business groups through nomenklatura appointments, confirming Pearson's view of a regulatory state run on Leninist norms.
Extends Pearson's earlier picture of party control over strategic sectors to explain why party-state capitalism provokes foreign securitization.
Tests performance legitimacy directly: free rural schooling raised central-government support only where citizens credited Beijing for it.
Shows the politicized anticorruption campaign carries a legitimacy cost, as local investigations lower rather than raise regime support.
The book generalizes the regime-insecurity explanation of Chinese territorial compromise to all of China's border disputes.
Shows NGO ratings can raise local compliance with central environmental mandates, a bottom-up complement to the recentralization Kostka and Nahm describe.
Argues propaganda keeps citizens in line by signaling regime strength, not by persuading them as the thought-work account assumes.
Identifies the cost of signaling through propaganda: hard propaganda lowers trust in state messages even as it displays power.
Finds crude, overt propaganda backfires, a scope condition on Stockmann's claim that commercialized media sustain regime support.
Shows lineage leaders in office are co-opted to ease land takings, a dark side of the solidary-group accountability Tsai identified.
Lineage officeholders may raise public goods, as Xu and Yao find, yet they also weaken villagers' property rights.
Formalizes when tolerating public voice yields information without collective-action risk, extending Lorentzen's logic of strategic censorship.
Gives a theoretical rationale for the observed pattern of tolerating criticism while deleting calls for collective action.
Explains the timing and tools of Chinese coercion in the South China Sea that Fravel's strategy account describes.
Shows that when Beijing escalates over territory it favors calibrated non-military coercion, refining Fravel's account of when China uses force.
Shows how local governments suppress resistance through hired thugs, adding an outsourced channel to Cai's account of local suppression.
Like relational repression, subcontracted violence lets the state coerce through non-state agents while keeping deniability.
Shows consultative channels come with targeted censorship relief on the policy under discussion, specifying how consultative authoritarianism works online.
Tests the claim that autocrats open voice when they want information, using censorship changes during consultation periods.
Applies the coercive-institutions dilemma between foreign and domestic threats to the CCP's control of the PLA and paramilitary police.
Finds factional influence on provincial decisions fell after Xi's purge, a time-bound limit on factional models of Chinese policy.
Measures the downstream effect of the politicized anticorruption purge on factional decision making in the provinces.
List experiments show trust in the center is inflated by social desirability yet still high, qualifying survey-based trust estimates since Shi.
Finds limited preference falsification in trust questions, narrowing worries that Chinese survey support is largely feigned.
Shows public support for the social credit system Liang describes depends on state framing that casts it as anti-fraud rather than surveillance.
Measures how the state's public-opinion management shapes citizens' acceptance of digital social-management tools.
Shows petitioners win by disruptive troublemaking that threatens stability, a tactic beyond rightful resistance's appeal to official commitments.
The book generalizes the troublemaking-as-leverage argument into a theory of contentious authoritarianism.
Shows the patriotic-education machinery Wang described is ramped up when domestic popular threats rise.
Documents a decentralized, entertainment-style state presence on Douyin, extending participatory persuasion to short-video platforms.
Moves from fabricated posts to thousands of official accounts, showing state content production on social media at far larger scale.
Like Fravel's regime-insecurity logic, shows external relations and threats shaped how Beijing managed ethnic frontier groups.
Explains Xinjiang's turn to mass preventive repression through perceived external terrorist links, echoing Han and Mylonas's external-threat logic of ethnic policy.
Builds on Bovingdon's history of oscillating Xinjiang policy to explain the post-2014 shift to mass internment.
Situates Xinjiang's high-tech surveillance in the long cycle of coercion and inducement Bovingdon traced.
Generalizes the patron-client structure Oi found in rural grain politics to authority relations in the urban work unit.
Tracks how the identity cleavage central to The Taiwan Voter combines with pragmatic threat calculations on cross-strait policy through 2020.
Extends the idea that disruption gives the weak leverage to lumpenproletarian groups such as street vendors and informal workers.
Explains the failure of Chinese anti-bribery websites through the state's restraint on online collective action that King, Pan and Roberts document.
Shows local congress deputies serve as informational conduits for autocrats, extending the consultative-institution logic to elected representatives.
Like Manion, treats Chinese congress deputies as channels of information that make autocracy more responsive without accountability.
Shows the stability-maintenance apparatus extends into social assistance, with dibao targeted at people flagged as threats.
Generalizes the elite-capture finding into a theory of how the party co-opts civil society to control villages.
Extends relational repression from individual protesters to the systematic infiltration of lineage and religious groups.
Explains the returns to legislative office Truex found: entrepreneurs seek seats to shield property from predatory local officials.
Shows how private entrepreneurs' ties to the state, rather than democratic demands, secure their interests.
Resolves Wedeman's double paradox by unbundling corruption and showing access money can coexist with growth.
Applies Ang's coevolutionary account of Chinese development to the types and effects of corruption.
Confirms with randomized posts and participant observation that collective-action potential, not criticism, triggers censorship.
Shows growth performance raises promotion odds mainly for connected provincial leaders, conditioning the tournament model.
Finds connections and performance are complements, reconciling factional and meritocratic accounts of advancement.
Explains why unregistered NGOs survive under graduated controls: local officials tolerate them while they fill welfare gaps and stay apolitical.
Like Spires, finds NGOs survive through accommodation with local officials, here shown in registration decisions.
Shows the micro-practices of protest bargaining and payoffs through which local officials regularize unrest.
Details how grassroots officials buy stability through concessions, the bargaining Cai's power-structure account of protest outcomes implies.
Shows princeling-linked firms lost land-price discounts under the anticorruption campaign, evidence on what the politicized campaign targeted.
Shows county leaders time spending to their promotion windows, a fiscal mechanism behind career-incentive models.
Shows local leaders' short time horizons undercut the authoritarian environmentalism Gilley described.
Traces how the social credit system extends the data-driven social management Creemers identified.
Applies Fravel's framework on territorial disputes to China's delaying strategy in the South China Sea.
Shows digital surveillance lets the security state substitute targeted repression for broad co-optation.
